this year i quit my full-time job with no backup plan, moved across 4 cities, took 40 flights, lived in a basement for 2 months, and raised a million dollars to start a company with my best friends. most eventful, albeit stupid, year of my life. here’s what i learned:

1. you have way more to gain than lose, as long as you’re cool losing first. being young means you can afford to fail. no mortgage, no kids, no real responsibilities yet. this is literally the only time in your life where you can make completely insane career moves and it won’t ruin you. the fear is always worse than the reality.

2. you only really learn by screwing up. reading about something and actually doing it are completely different. you can study business all you want, but you don’t actually know how to build one until you’ve tried and failed. friction is where the real education happens.

3. success costs your freedom, freedom costs your ego. the biggest thing holding me back this year was caring what people thought. posting content where everyone i know can see it felt humiliating at first. but that embarrassment? that’s the price of admission. once you pay it, everything else gets easier.

4. boring work is harder than hard work. most people think success comes from solving complex problems or being smart. it doesn’t. it comes from doing the tedious, repetitive, unglamorous stuff that smart people think they’re too good for. that’s the real filter.

5. the people you’re with matter more than anything else. nothing else even comes close.

hope this helps someone

feeling generous for my 24th year of life…so here’s 10 things you can start doing TODAY to become a better speaker 

1. listen closer - being intentional about listening to how others sound will help you improve how YOU sound
2. care more - recognize the importance of this skill…it literally determines every single aspect of your life
3. remove your insecurities - everyone is afraid. do it scared. 
4. get into running - running, like speaking, is about the mind, not the technique.
5. practice daily - speaking is like working out. you have to do it with discipline. 
6. practice extemporaneously - get good at speaking off the top of your head, not memorizing scripts. 
7. record yourself daily - listening to yourself is crucial. even if it is uncomfortable. 
8. breathe - so much of speaking poorly has to do with thinking poorly. breath, pace yourself, speak. 
9. perform - every time you open your mouth to utter a word, you are perfuming. Treat it as such 
10. join the waitlist (www.speakeasy.run)

challenging communication is less of an emotional problem than it is a technical problem. there’s a reason they’re called difficult conversations — they’re difficult for everyone. nobody goes through any form of challenging communication completely comfortably. everyone experiences fear and anxiety and stress with every word they utter. the difference is in those words. people who know how to speak their minds and voice their opinions aren’t any more comfortable doing it than you - they just have a better grasp on how they speak, what they’re saying, and what the listener is thinking as they’re saying it. speaking really is everything man.

idk which self-help red pill podcast bro is responsible for this but “grinding” and “productivity” are not actual spikes. you can’t put work ethic or discipline as a skill on your resume.
instead of wasting your life and burning calories trying to win every day but working harder than the previous day, focus on the highest leverage skill a person can have: speaking and communicating well. then you’ll see actual results in your life, not just fake dopamine outcomes. my goal is to help you with that. 

#explore #advice #productivity #hardwork #discipline #communication #selfhelp

this is my official confession. i’m a fraud. and you can be one too. 

I could stand on top of Everest with a big ass sign emphasizing the importance of speaking and it still wouldn’t do enough justice for how much I believe in this skill. it’s such an easy way to stand out in literally any context, and it doesn’t take much to get there. I got so annoyed by the fact that nobody teaches this that I decided to quit my job and build an app for it. stay tuned.

cognitive offloading is a 6 syllable term for “you’re boring now”. 

we all know we’re getting stupider because of AI, but it’s hard to care because it’s hard to see. You can’t really observe how much it’s slowing you down when it’s speeding up so many of the things you don’t care about. Unfortunately, while it might be hard to see, it’s easy to hear. When your brain literally gets slower at active recall and information retrieval (12 syllables for “you’re dumb”), the first thing to go is your speaking. You become less fluid in speech, less interesting in conversation, more nervous in presentation. You might feel that and think it’s something you’ve always had, and it’s got nothing to do with AI. Maybe that’s true, but it’s something to care about regardless.

raised our first round, these are the things I’ve found to matter:

1. Problem: are you solving a real problem, or are you building a solution in search of a problem? with speakeasy, we’re solving a problem that even the investors we pitch to experience in their daily life. we’ve found that made it easy 
2. Solution: what’s the smallest, simplest version of a solution you can build, and what group of people would immediately pay for it? every idea starts with some grand vision for a fix all solution, but in practice we’ve already found that isn’t how it works 
3. Why Now: what combination of circumstances aligned to make this necessary NOW? a new technology? an emerging trend? a societal tailwind? if there’s isn’t an answer, there’s likely a reason this hasn’t worked.
4. Why You: what makes you and your team the perfect people suited for this. a hidden truth we’ve discovered is that passion is enough — it could be the case that you are the only person in the world that cares about this.

of course, none of this works without you being able to present it persuasively. luckily, im building something to help you with that:)

feel like this is a video I would’ve wanted in the beginning. there’s a lot of logistical noise you have to get through to make an idea more official, but it’s pretty easy now. In review, when you have an idea for a startup your first steps (outside of building the damn thing) should be: 

1. Incorporating the company (Stripe Atlas) 
2. Setting up SAFE’s & investor relation portals if you’re raising money (Carta + Pulley) 
3. Making a bank account (Mercury or any other bank works for this) 
4. Setting up accounting software (YNAB or Monarch Money or Quikbooks) 
5. Setting up basic project management & documentation tools (Linear, Notion, etc.) 
6. Building the mf business

You could probably do all of this in less than a few hours. It’s simpler than it seems and easier than it looks

recounting our first shoot 

this was one of those ‘trivial’ experiences that was weirdly meaningful for me personally (and probably no one else) 

this was about few months after we had really started the brand, and we needed to do an ‘official’ photoshoot for the insta + product announcements. for the others this was probably just a few hour task on a Saturday morning, but for me it was my first time ever seeing or doing a photoshoot of any kind

there’s this profound feeling you get when you take part in the creation of something that you’ve interacted with thousands of times before. I’ve seen a million product photos of models for brands throughout my life, and never really gave much thought to the process that goes into making those. and then I’m here, on this field, holding a deflector while we take photos of nich and don and learning to do it myself 

by far one of the coolest aspects of building a brand (or any company) is the realization that you can make most things happen without any expertise or experience. this could be something trivial, like a basic photoshoot, or something complex like an inventory management system. the real challenge is discerning which components of that process actually matter and which parts don’t. i think the reason this first photoshoot is so memorable for me is because it was the first time I encountered that feeling.

building in public is lame

at least from what i’ve seen, the concept of documenting the process of building a startup has become commodified to some degree — i feel like founders now treat it as another marketing channel to promote themselves or their company. 

ofc, this makes complete sense to me. some big consulting firm probably conducted some big user survey somewhere & reached the conclusion that adding a persona to a company is the new approach to growing an audience. but in my experience with trying this out myself over the past few months, i’ve been feeling a stark contrast between “documenting” and “creating”

saying all this to say that i realistically wont stay consistent on this account if i treat it like another marketing channel — we have no shortage of accounts for the brand or personal to do that on — so i figured id treat it as more like a curated finsta instead. my friends all know im a chronic overthinker. might as well put all those thoughts somewhere. 

the core experience of fortytwo, at least till this point, has never really been about building and maximizing our growth as a startup (though that this a major facet of it of course). in my experience its been more about figuring out the coolest things my friends and i can do together, trying to make that profitable, and making working actually fun. bc i refuse to believe anyone with a real job (me included) actually has fun with it. the content on this account should reflect that.
